# The Heat Is Uneven: How Cities Can Make Summer Bearable

Summer heat has become one of the defining challenges of urban life. Cities are inherently hotter than their surrounding countryside—the urban heat island effect can raise temperatures by several degrees, and climate change is pushing heat waves to become longer, more frequent, and more deadly. Yet the experience of that heat is remarkably uneven. A person walking down a tree-lined boulevard in Portland may feel ten degrees cooler than someone crossing a sun-baked parking lot a few blocks away. This unevenness is not accidental; it is the product of design choices, and it can be corrected by better ones. Cities that want to make summer heat bearable must invest in trees, redesign their streets, retrofit their housing, and expand public transit—while being honest about the tradeoffs these changes impose on residents.

## Trees: The Oldest and Best Technology

The single most effective tool against urban heat is also the oldest: shade. Trees cool cities in two ways. Their canopies block solar radiation before it hits pavement, and their leaves release water vapor through transpiration, cooling the surrounding air.
